# Debugging

Debugging a MoQ system means finding where progress stops between the publisher and the player. A black screen can result from a connection failure, a missing track, unusable media, or a presentation problem.

Follow the path below until you find the first step that isn’t working. We’ll go through the checks in that order, then investigate a player that falls behind or freezes and gather what we need for a bug report.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Locate the first missing step in playback
  accDescr: Check transport, session, discovery, subscription, object delivery, decoding, and presentation in order. A failure at each stage narrows which layer to investigate.
  A["Transport connects"] --> B["MoQ session opens"]
  B --> N["Publication and track found"]
  N --> C["Subscription accepted"]
  C --> D["Objects arrive"]
  D --> E["Decoder produces frames"]
  E --> F["Player presents frames"]
```

For example, if objects arrive but the decoder produces no frames, changing the relay address is unlikely to help. Start with the media format and decoder configuration. If decoded frames exist but the screen stays black, investigate presentation instead.

## The transport never connects

Check the endpoint address, certificate trust, listener, and network path. For a QUIC path, confirm UDP reachability. A successful HTTPS request to the same hostname may only prove TCP reachability.

If the application uses a fallback, log which transport won. Test from outside the server’s local network before concluding that a public endpoint works. Separate a certificate error from a timeout; their remedies are different.

## The session opens, but nothing appears

Confirm protocol compatibility and the scope or path the client joined. Then verify that the publication actually exists and the client is authorized to discover it. A connected client looking in the wrong namespace can wait forever without any packet loss.

Check the exact name bytes when working close to MOQT. Similar-looking text is not necessarily the same identifier. At the library level, inspect any normalization or path-prefix rules.

## The track is found, but objects do not arrive

Look for subscription acceptance or a specific rejection. Confirm the publisher is producing the requested track and the relay has an upstream source. Discovery of a publication is not proof that every expected track is available.

When you find an error, record where it came from as well as its code. A `REQUEST_ERROR` rejects one request, a stream reset ends one stream, and a session error closes the MoQ session. For example, a `DELIVERY_TIMEOUT` reset on video may leave audio running. These use separate error tables in [draft-21 §12](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-12), so the same number can mean different things depending on where it appears. moq-lite may expose different errors.

Check filters, cancellation, and request lifetime. An accidentally closed subscription can look like a stalled network. If objects are requested from history, verify they remain retained; live availability does not imply old-object availability.

## Objects arrive, but media does not play

Inspect the catalog, selected codec, decoder configuration, and the first usable decoding point. Starting with a predicted frame whose references are missing can fail even when delivery is perfect.

Then inspect decoding and presentation separately. Are decoded frames being produced? Is audio blocked by playback policy? Is the renderer waiting on a timestamp far in the future? Does a hidden tab change the scheduling behavior?

Try a media sample that you know works with this player. If it plays while the live source fails, compare their encoder settings and packaging before changing the transport.

## Playback works, but keeps falling behind

Watch the queues and playback delay over time, and compare the source bitrate with the rate arriving at the player. If the source keeps producing more than the connection can carry, check whether the player switches renditions or skips old content.

Watch the spikes too. A large keyframe can briefly fill a queue even when the average bitrate fits. Check how long that queue takes to drain.

The player may also retain stale decoded frames after the transport has recovered. Measure network arrival time and actual display time independently where possible.

## Turn a symptom into a test

Suppose the picture freezes while audio continues. Start by writing two facts: audio is still being presented; video is not. That narrows the investigation, but it does not prove the network is healthy. Audio may need less bandwidth, and the two media paths may have different queues.

| Question | If yes | If no |
|---|---|---|
| Are new video objects arriving? | Inspect parsing and decoding | Inspect the video subscription and publisher |
| Are decoded video frames being produced? | Inspect presentation timing and rendering | Check configuration and missing reference pictures |
| Are decoded frames waiting past their scheduled display times? | Inspect the playback queue, clock, and rendering | Trace the missing picture through arrival, parsing, and decoding |

A frozen picture gets older whether the cause is missing data, a decoder failure, or stalled rendering. Its age alone cannot tell you which queue is responsible. Check these counters over the same time interval. A decoder that produced frames a minute ago might have stopped since then. If a stage has no counter, add a log there so you can see whether data is getting through.

## Collect evidence that connects the layers

For a useful bug report, record the client and relay versions, actual transport, publication and track identifiers, codec, error code, and the time of the failure. Include the smallest repeatable sequence that triggers it.

QUIC packet captures do not normally expose encrypted application payloads. Structured application logs and transport telemetry such as qlog can provide information that packet timing alone cannot. If your implementation exports a supported qlog trace, [qvis](https://qvis.quictools.info/) provides QUIC visualizations for inspecting transport behavior. A transport trace still does not show whether the player presented a frame. Redact credentials and private publication names before sharing evidence.

One final habit helps: change one thing at a time. If you replace the codec, relay, browser, and network together, a successful run will leave you with four possible explanations.
